summary: This informational RFC describes Sakai-Kasahara Key Encryption (SAKKE), which uses identity-based encryption so a sender can pass a shared secret to a receiver. The receiver's identity serves as the public key. It is published for information rather than as a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: In public key cryptography, a sender needs the receiver's public key, and that key usually has to be fetched and then trusted. Identity-based encryption removes the fetch: the receiver's identity string, such as an email address, is enough. SAKKE is an identity-based scheme built on elliptic curve pairings, published as an Informational document.

questions: how does identity based encryption work
what is a shared secret value
how does sakke use bilinear pairings
subtitle: An identity-based encryption scheme where the receiver's identity string is enough for the sender to send it a shared secret.

tldr.problem: In public key cryptography, a sender needs the receiver's public key, which usually means fetching it and trusting whoever supplied it. Identity-based encryption removes that step, but needed an efficient scheme.
tldr.mechanism: SAKKE uses bilinear pairings on a supersingular elliptic curve. The Key Management Service derives a private key from the receiver's Identifier, and the sender encapsulates a random shared secret against that Identifier using only public parameters.
tldr.outcome: The sender needs only the receiver's identity string and the KMS public key, and the sending operation involves no pairing computation, which also makes group communication cheaper.

facts.label: Shared secret range
facts.value: An integer in the range 0 to (2^n) - 1

facts.label: Identifier range
facts.value: An integer in the range 2 to q-1

today: RFC 6508 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no obsoleting and no updating RFC. It publishes a usable algorithm rather than a Standards Track specification, and it is the scheme that RFC 6507 is designed to authenticate within.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document defines an efficient use of Identity-Based Encryption (IBE) based on bilinear pairings. The Sakai-Kasahara IBE cryptosystem is described for establishment of a shared secret value. It adds to the IBE options available in RFC 5091, providing an efficient primitive and an additional family of curves.

The document is restricted to a particular family of curves, the supersingular curves with equation y^2 = x^3 - 3 * x modulo p, which have the benefit of a simple and efficient method of calculating the pairing the cryptosystem is based on.

IBE schemes allow public and private keys to be derived from Identifiers. In fact the Identifier can itself be viewed as corresponding to a public key or a certificate in a traditional public key system. In IBE, however, the Identifier can be formed by both the Sender and the Receiver, which obviates the necessity of providing public keys through a third party or of transmitting certified public keys during each session establishment. Furthermore, in an IBE system, calculation of keys can occur as needed, and indeed messages can be sent to users who are yet to enroll.

The Sakai-Kasahara primitive described here supports simplex transmission of messages from a Sender to a Receiver, and the choice of elliptic curve pairing on which the primitive is based allows simple and efficient implementations. The SAKKE scheme is drawn from the Sakai-Kasahara Key Encapsulation Mechanism scheme, as modified to support multi-party communications, submitted to the IEEE P1363 Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary public key encryption needs the recipient's public key, which normally has to be looked up and then trusted. Identity-based encryption removes the lookup: the recipient's identity string, such as an email address, is enough to encrypt to them. SAKKE is one identity-based scheme, built on elliptic curve pairings and published as an Informational document.

sections.title: Definitions: Identifiers, Keys and the Shared Secret
sections.content:
Each user of an IBE system must have a unique, unambiguous identifying string that can be easily derived by all valid communicants. This string is the user's Identifier, and in SAKKE it is an integer in the range 2 to q-1. The method by which Identifiers are formed must be defined for each application.

The Key Management Service (KMS) is a trusted third party for the IBE system. It derives system secrets and distributes key material to those authorized to obtain it. Applications may support mutual communication between users of multiple KMSs, denoted KMS_T, KMS_S and so on. The public parameters are a set of parameters held by all users of the IBE system; each application of SAKKE must define them, and the parameters needed are p, q, E, P, g = <P,P>, Hash and n.

Three keys carry the scheme. The Master Secret z_T is the master key generated and privately kept by KMS_T, used to generate the private keys of the users it provisions; it is an integer in the range 2 to q-1. The KMS Public Key Z_T = [z_T]P is used to form the public key establishment keys for all users provisioned by KMS_T; it is a point of order q in E(F_p) and must be provisioned to all who are authorized to send messages to users of the IBE system. The Receiver Secret Key is what each enrolled user is provisioned with by its KMS; the RSK provided to a user with Identifier 'a' by KMS_T is denoted K_(a,T), and in SAKKE it is a point of order q in E(F_p).

What travels is the Shared Secret Value and the Encapsulated Data. The aim of the scheme is for the Sender to securely transmit a shared secret value to the Receiver; the SSV is an integer in the range 0 to (2^n) - 1. The Encapsulated Data are used to transmit that secret information securely, and can be computed directly from the Receiver's Identifier, the public parameters, the KMS Public Key and the SSV to be transmitted. In SAKKE the Encapsulated Data are a point of order q in E(F_p) and an integer in the range 0 to (2^n) - 1.

Because the curve equation and the pairing are constant and used for all applications, hosts must agree on the values of n, p, q, P = (P_x,P_y), g = <P,P> and Hash. Each application must either define an application-specific constant value for each of them or define a mechanism for hosts to negotiate a value.
sections.plainLanguage: The pieces are: an identity string that is really a number, a central service that holds a master secret and hands out per-user private keys, a public key that anyone can use to send to that service's users, and a random secret value that the sender wraps up for the receiver.

sections.title: Curves, Pairings and Representations
sections.content:
The curve E is a supersingular elliptic curve of j-invariant 1728. E(F_p) contains a cyclic subgroup of order q, denoted E(F_p)[q], while the larger object E(F_p^2) contains the direct product of two cyclic subgroups of order q, denoted E(F_p^2)[q]. The point P is a generator of E(F_p)[q], specified by the affine coordinates (P_x,P_y) in F_p that satisfy the curve equation.

The extension field F_p^2 is F_p[i], where i^2 + 1 = 0. If (Q_x,Q_y) are affine coordinates in F_p for a point Q on E(F_p)[q], then (-Q_x, iQ_y) are affine coordinates in F_p^2 for a point on E(F_p^2)[q], denoted [i]Q. The two points P and [i]P together generate E(F_p^2)[q], and the map [i] is sometimes called the distortion map.

The pairing used is a version of the Tate-Lichtenbaum pairing, a bilinear map from E(F_p)[q] cross E(F_p)[q] onto the subgroup of order q in PF_p, where PF_p is the projectivization of F_p, that is (F_p^2)*/(F_p)*, a cyclic group of order p + 1. It satisfies the bilinear relation <[x]R,Q> = <R,[x]Q> = <R,Q>^x for all integers x. The RFC gives pseudocode for computing it, making use of Barreto's trick for avoiding the calculation of denominators. It notes that the pairing can also be computed without any explicit reference to the extension field F_p^2, which reduces the number and complexity of the operations needed.

Canonical representations are fixed so that implementations interoperate. Integers are represented as octet strings with a bit length that is a multiple of 8, most significant bit first and padded with zero bits on the left. Elements of F_p are represented as integers in the range 0 to p-1 with octet string length L = Ceiling(lg(p)/8). Elements of PF_p are represented as an element of F_p and are L octets in length. Elliptic curve points are represented in uncompressed form as 0x04 || x' || y', which is 2*L+1 octets in length. The Encapsulated Data are represented as an elliptic curve point concatenated with an integer in the range 0 to (2^n) - 1, giving a total length of 2*L + n + 1 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme uses a special kind of elliptic curve chosen so that the pairing, the operation that ties the two sides together, is cheap to compute. The RFC also fixes the byte layout of every value, so that two implementations produce identical results.

sections.title: The SAKKE Cryptosystem
sections.content:
Setup. All users share a set of public parameters with a KMS. In most circumstances a system will use a single KMS, but users provisioned by different KMSs can interoperate if they use a common set of public parameters and each possesses the necessary KMS Public Keys. To facilitate this, parameters are expected to be published in application-specific standards. KMS_T chooses its KMS Master Secret z_T by randomly selecting a value in the range 2 to q-1, and derives its KMS Public Key by performing Z_T = [z_T]P. It then derives each RSK from an Identifier and its Master Secret: for Identifier 'a' the RSK K_(a,T) must be derived as K_(a,T) = [(a + z_T)^-1]P, where 'a' is interpreted as an integer and the inversion is performed modulo q.

User provisioning. The KMS must provide its KMS Public Key to all users through an authenticated channel, and RSKs must be supplied through a channel that provides confidentiality and mutual authentication; the mechanisms that secure those channels are beyond the scope of the document and are application specific. On receipt of key material, each user must verify its RSK, which for Identifier 'a' is done by checking that < [a]P + Z, K_(a,T) > = g.

Sender. The Sender forms Encapsulated Data and sends them to the Receiver, who processes them, and the result is a shared secret that can be used as keying material for securing further communications. Write the Sender as A with Identifier 'a' and the Receiver as B with Identifier 'b', with A provisioned by KMS_T and B by KMS_S. To form Encapsulated Data for B, A needs to hold Z_S. The Sender selects a random ephemeral integer value for the SSV in the range 0 to 2^n - 1; computes r = HashToIntegerRange(SSV || b, q, Hash); computes R_(b,S) = [r]([b]P + Z_S) in E(F_p); computes the Hint H, by computing g^r and then H := SSV XOR HashToIntegerRange(g^r, 2^n, Hash); forms the Encapsulated Data (R_(b,S), H) and transmits them to B; and outputs the SSV for use to derive key material for the application to be keyed.

Receiver. Device B receives the Encapsulated Data from A and processes them using its RSK K_(b,S), provisioned in advance by KMS_S. The Receiver parses the Encapsulated Data to extract R_(b,S) and H; computes w := < R_(b,S), K_(b,S) >, which by bilinearity equals g^r; computes SSV = H XOR HashToIntegerRange(w, 2^n, Hash); computes r = HashToIntegerRange(SSV || b, q, Hash); computes TEST = [r]([b]P + Z_S) in E(F_p) and, if TEST does not equal R_(b,S), must not use the SSV to derive key material; and outputs the SSV for use to derive key material for the application to be keyed.

Group communications. The scheme can be used to exchange SSVs for group communications. To provide a shared secret to multiple Receivers, a Sender must form Encapsulated Data for each of their Identifiers and transmit the appropriate data to each Receiver. Any party possessing the group SSV may extend the group by forming Encapsulated Data for a new group member. While the Sender needs to form multiple Encapsulated Data, the sending operation avoids pairings, so extending to multiple Receivers is more efficient than for alternative IBE schemes that require the Sender to compute a pairing.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender picks a random secret, mixes it with the receiver's identity number, and sends two values: a curve point and a scrambled version of the secret. Only the receiver's private key can unscramble it. The sender never computes the pairing, which is why sending to a group of receivers is cheaper than in schemes that need it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security provided by the algorithm depends entirely on the secrecy of the secret keys it uses, and for an adversary to defeat that security it is assumed that computationally intensive cryptanalytic attacks will be needed to recover a secret key. A security proof exists for SAKKE in the Random Oracle Model.

When defining public parameters, guidance on parameter sizes from SP 800-57 should be followed. The size of the F_p^2 discrete logarithm on which the security rests is 2*lg(p). If k bits of security are needed, then lg(q) should be chosen to be at least 2*k, and a hash with an output size of at least 2*k should be chosen.

The KMS Master Secret provides the security for each device provisioned by the KMS and must not be revealed to any other entity. Each user's RSK protects the SAKKE communications it receives and must not be revealed to any entity other than the trusted KMS and the authorized user. To ensure that the RSK is received only by an authorized device, it must be provided through a secure channel, and the security offered by the system is no greater than the security provided by that delivery channel.

IBE systems have different properties from other asymmetric schemes with regard to key recovery. The KMS, and hence any administrator with appropriate privileges, can create RSKs for arbitrary Identifiers, and procedures to monitor the creation of RSKs, such as logging of administrator actions, should be defined by any functioning implementation of SAKKE. Identifiers must be defined unambiguously by each application, and it is not necessary to hash the data in a format for Identifiers except where its size would be greater than that of q, so weaknesses caused by collisions in hash functions can be avoided without reliance on the structure of the Identifier format. Applications may include a time and date component in their Identifier format, to ensure that Identifiers, and hence RSKs, are only valid for a fixed period of time.

The randomness of the values stipulated to be selected at random is essential to the security provided by SAKKE. If the ephemeral value r selected by the Sender is not chosen at random, the SSV used to provide key material for further communications could be predictable.
sections.plainLanguage: The security rests on the master secret, each user's private key and the randomness of the sender's choice. One property of identity-based systems is worth noting: the central service can create a private key for any identity string, so a working implementation should log what its administrators do.

messages.label: RSK K_(b,S)
messages.note: The private key derived from the Receiver's Identifier, delivered over a confidential channel.

messages.label: KMS Public Key Z_S
messages.note: The public value the Sender needs in order to encrypt to users of that KMS.

messages.label: Encapsulated Data (R_(b,S), H)
messages.note: The point and the hint that let only the Receiver recover the shared secret.

items.title: Identifier
items.text: The user's unique identifying string, an integer in the range 2 to q-1.

items.title: Master Secret
items.text: The integer z_T kept privately by the KMS, used to derive user keys.

items.title: KMS Public Key
items.text: Z_T = [z_T]P, the public value that lets anyone encrypt to the KMS's users.

items.title: Receiver Secret Key
items.text: K_(a,T) = [(a + z_T)^-1]P, the point only the Receiver holds.

items.title: Shared Secret Value
items.text: The integer in the range 0 to (2^n) - 1 that both sides end up with.

items.title: Encapsulated Data
items.text: A curve point and an integer, 2*L + n + 1 octets in total.
